Far-right party National Rally (RN) candidate in France's 2027 presidential election Marine Le Pen, flanked by RN President Jordan Bardella, right, and far-right ally party Union des droites pour la Republique (UDR) leader Eric Ciotti, left, at a campaign kickoff rally in Orleans, central France, on October 25, 2026 [AFP]By Virginia PietromarchiPublished On 25 Oct 202625 Oct 2026
Orleans, France – Marine Le Pen took to the stage with a clear message: She would lead France’s “renaissance” as the country sank into crisis – and she would do so soon.
The far-right figure’s words were met with cheers from thousands of supporters gathered in Orleans in central France on Sunday, as she launched her presidential campaign against a backdrop of mass demonstrations and widespread social and economic discontent.

“Marine présidente!” the crowd chanted, waving French flags beneath a sea of red and blue lights. Organisers said 8,500 supporters had gathered in a venue transformed into a fort for the event.
Standing tall on stage in a pink blazer, her hair impeccably coiffed, Le Pen spoke with the confidence of a leader who believes the presidency is within reach.
Riding high in the polls, with candidates from the right, left and centre trailing behind her, she presented the election as a historic opportunity to restore France’s past glory.
“This is a story to be written, a destiny to be fulfilled,” she told the crowd, which erupted in cheers.

US President Donald Trump walks past Attorney General Todd Blanche at the White House on October 21 [Alex Brandon/AP Photo]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 25 Oct 202625 Oct 2026
United States Attorney General Todd Blanche has defended the Department of Justice’s decision to sue to prevent the certification of a Republican loss in Alaska’s tight Senate race.
On Sunday, Blanche did a tour of the morning political shows in the US, making stops at CNN’s State of the Union TV programme and CBS’s Face the Nation.
Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Trump’s approval ratings plummet: what that means for the US midtermslist 2 of 3Trump administration sues to block possible Democratic win in Alaskalist 3 of 3Dan Sullivan vs Dan Sullivan: Why is Trump’s DOJ suing in Alaska?end of list
In each appearance, he faced pointed questions about the legality of the Justice Department’s efforts, responding, in some cases, with open frustration.
“ Why is this controversial?” Blanche asked CNN host Dana Bash at one point. He proceeded to accuse one of the candidates in the Senate race of intentionally trying to confuse voters.
“We’re going to try to create a situation where that can be remedied,” he said. “That shouldn’t be something that is causing this shock and horror.”
But the Justice Department’s lawsuit, filed on October 22, has been the subject of bipartisan criticism.
Many have accused President Donald Trump’s administration of laying the groundwork to block a Democratic win in the race. Trump himself claimed to have authorised the lawsuit.
“I’m the one who said do it,” he told reporters on Friday.

Kenyan police officers look on as a bus involved in a deadly collision with a truck on the Nairobi-Mombasa Highway sits at a police station in Makueni County, Kenya, on October 25, 2026 [AP Photo]By Al Jazeera Staff and APPublished On 25 Oct 202625 Oct 2026
A bus carrying mourners has collided with a truck on a major highway in southeastern Kenya, killing at least 24 people, police say.
The crash happened in the Kanga area near Mtito Andei, on the road linking the capital, Nairobi, to the coastal city of Mombasa, at about 7:45am (04:45 GMT) on Sunday, October 25.
Recommended Stories list of 2 itemslist 1 of 2Uganda orders 21-day Ebola quarantine for citizens returning from DR Congolist 2 of 2Kenya announces second Ebola death, says ‘no evidence’ of community spreadend of list
Another 24 people were injured, hospital officials said.
The deaths came just over three weeks after another crash on the highway killed 17 people, prompting fresh government promises to improve road safety.
The bus belonged to Power of the Word Church International in Mombasa and was taking passengers home from their pastor’s funeral in western Kenya.
They had stopped for breakfast shortly before the collision, according to one survivor.
The other vehicle was a truck transporting cement.
Violet Mwandonyi, who survived the crash, told the Associated Press on Sunday that she remembered passengers crying out for passing motorists to help.
She said she did not know what had happened to her two children, who had been travelling on the bus.
The cause of the crash remains under investigation.

Manchester United manager Michael Carrick left the Old Trafford pitch on Sunday to the sound of his name being sung by the adoring home support, but he may never lead the team onto the field again.

item.title: The narrative battle over France’s unrest
item.description:
play video
play video
Video Duration play-arrow
Student protests, police violence and French media obsessed with 'barbarians'.Read more
What began as protests over education has rapidly taken over the streets of France and turned into one of the country’s biggest waves of unrest in years.
Many mainstream media outlets have focused their coverage on the violence and looting rather than on the demands of the demonstrators. A lot of airtime has fixated on who the protesters are and what they look like, often using racist terms. That narrative has been picked up by right-wing movements abroad.
Contributors:
Cole Stangler – author, Paris Is Not Dead, and lecturer, American College of the Mediterranean
Diane de Vignemont – Paris-based journalist
Harrison Stetler – lecturer and writer
Philippe Marliere – professor of French and European politics, University College London
On our radar
Israel’s elections are just days away and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has reverted to a familiar alarmist tactic to consolidate support: hyping an “imminent” threat from Iran and telling the United States that it should “finish the job”. Meenakshi Ravi looks at the messaging.
Olga Rudenko: Independent journalism is the ‘ultimate patriotic act’
More than four and a half years into Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukraine remains under attack, and its journalists are forced to balance many responsibilities at once.
They are documenting a war that has become more dangerous than ever, countering Russian propaganda efforts and trying to hold their own government to account at a time when the news media have been expected to fall into line. The Kyiv Independent, an online newspaper, has been doing all three since 2021.
The Listening Post spoke with its editor-in-chief and cofounder Olga Rudenko about the pressures of reporting when your country is at war.

Casting her ballot at a polling station in Belgrade on Sunday [Marko Djurica/Reuters]By Al Jazeera StaffPublished On 25 Oct 202625 Oct 2026
Polls have closed in Serbia’s snap parliamentary election, which saw the highest voter turnout in decades, with a student-backed movement seeking to unseat longtime leader Aleksandar Vucic.
Voting ended at 8pm local time (19:00 GMT) on Sunday, with first indications of the result expected a few hours later.
Recommended Stories list of 2 itemslist 1 of 2Serbia votes in election pitting longtime leader against student movementlist 2 of 2Serbia votes as student-led bloc challenges longtime leader Vucicend of list
The vote will determine whether Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party (SNS), which has governed since 2012, can retain power against a movement born from nationwide anticorruption protests.
The State Election Commission said that voter turnout had reached 64.9 percent by 17:00GMT, ⁠⁠the ⁠⁠highest since ⁠⁠the breakup ‌‌of Yugoslavia in ‌‌1992.
The higher turnout does not show which side gained support.
University of Belgrade researcher Jelena Vasiljevic told Al Jazeera in an interview published on Friday that the SNS had a reliable voter base, while the students needed to attract people who normally did not vote.
Sunday’s voting was also marked by reports of intimidation and procedural problems.
The Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability (CRTA), an independent election watchdog, said its observers recorded pressure on voters or election workers at almost a third of the 500 polling stations it monitored.
It also reported failures to protect ballot secrecy.
